CausalChain: Chronic HBV/HCV infection -> Dysregulated m6A regulators (elevated METTL3, imbalanced FTO) -> Aberrant m6A modifications on viral, tumor-suppressor, and oncogenic mRNAs -> YTHDF2-mediated transcript decay and altered translation, leading to destabilization of tumor suppressors, enhanced oncogene activity, and metabolic reprogramming -> Impaired immune surveillance and establishment of an immune-tolerant, pro-oncogenic microenvironment -> Liver carcinogenesis
Hypothesis: In HBV/HCV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma, chronic viral infection induces dysregulation of the m6A RNA modification machinery, characterized by increased METTL3 and dysregulated FTO activities. This dysregulation simultaneously alters m6A modifications on host tumor suppressor mRNAs, key viral transcripts, and oncogenic/metabolic regulators (e.g., HIF-1α, BMI1), leading to their aberrant stabilization, decay or translational reprogramming via YTHDF2 and other m6A reader proteins. The net effect is a dual mechanism: (1) the destabilization of tumor suppressors and metabolic reprogramming that furthers oncogenesis, and (2) a compromised antiviral immune response that facilitates viral persistence and promotes an immune-tolerant tumor microenvironment. Utilizing advanced molecular profiling techniques (such as RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing and single-cell RNA-seq) alongside emerging epitranscriptomic editing tools (e.g., CRISPR-dCas systems targeting m6A sites), we propose that targeted correction of aberrant m6A marks can restore mRNA homeostasis and immune competence, thereby offering a novel therapeutic strategy for HBV/HCV-associated HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development in patients with chronic HBV/HCV infection involves multifaceted alterations in RNA epitranscriptomic regulation. Our revised hypothesis posits that chronic viral infection triggers dysregulation in m6A machinery, notably through overexpression of METTL3 and an imbalance in FTO activity, which not only destabilizes host tumor suppressor mRNAs via YTHDF2-mediated decay but also aberrantly modifies viral and oncogenic transcripts. These modifications lead to both a metabolic reprogramming of cancer cells and an immune-tolerant microenvironment. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as high-throughput m6A-RIP sequencing, CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic editing, and single-cell RNA profiling, we propose that precise manipulation of m6A marks can restore mRNA homeostasis, reinvigorate antiviral immunity, and offer a novel therapeutic strategy against HBV/HCV-associated HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis emphasized a dual effect of m6A dysregulation in destabilizing host tumor suppressor mRNAs and modifying viral transcripts to undermine antiviral immunity, leading to an immune-tolerant environment that promotes oncogenesis. The revised hypothesis preserves these core aspects but expands upon them by integrating additional mechanistic components: (1) It specifies the involvement of elevated METTL3 and imbalanced FTO, which tie directly to the original observation of dysregulated m6A regulators. (2) It clearly includes the role of YTHDF2 in mediating transcript decay, reinforcing the link between aberrant m6A modifications and mRNA destabilization. (3) It incorporates the impact on oncogenic and metabolic regulators (e.g., HIF-1α, BMI1), addressing observed phenomena related to cell proliferation and metabolic reprogramming. (4) It introduces contemporary technological approaches (high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic editing, single-cell profiling) to propose a practical pathway for therapeutic intervention and experimental validation. Each step of the original causal chain is explicitly reflected in the revised causal sequence, ensuring that the hypothesis remains innovative while addressing gaps highlighted in recent observations.
